rows: Measles is highly infectious and suspected cases require prompt public-health assessment.
Registered medical practitioners must urgently notify suspected measles through the required pathway.
Oral-fluid testing supports confirmation and national surveillance of suspected cases.
Case management includes determining the infectious period and identifying relevant exposure settings.
Contacts are risk assessed according to exposure, susceptibility and vulnerability.
MMR vaccination is the principal preventive measure against measles.
Vulnerable contacts can require urgent specialist public-health action.
UKHSA guidance supports warn-and-inform communication and outbreak control.
A regional case count or exposure notice does not prove infection in a specific individual.
Case and contact conclusions require current clinical, vaccination, laboratory and public-health evidence.
Pertussis is a bacterial respiratory infection and is notifiable in England and Wales.
Young infants are at greatest risk of severe complications.
Vaccination reduces the risk of serious disease and transmission.
Clinical and public-health management considers symptom onset, infectious period and laboratory testing.
Antibiotic treatment can reduce infectiousness when given within the relevant period.
Eligible close contacts may require prophylaxis according to current guidance.
Pregnancy vaccination helps protect babies before they complete their own primary vaccinations.
Health protection teams assess clusters and settings where vulnerable contacts may have been exposed.
A cough or notification in a locality does not establish pertussis in a particular person.
Management decisions require current clinical, laboratory, timing, contact and vaccination information.
Dengue is mainly transmitted through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes.
Travel risk varies by destination, season and current local transmission.
Mosquito-bite prevention includes repellent, covering exposed skin and suitable accommodation barriers.
Daytime bite precautions are important because Aedes mosquitoes often feed during daylight hours.
Travellers should seek destination-specific health advice before travel.
Fever or unusual illness during or after travel should prompt medical assessment with travel history disclosed.
Severe dengue can develop in a minority of infections and requires urgent clinical care.
UKHSA surveillance monitors travel-associated dengue infections.
Travel to a dengue-risk country does not establish infection.
Individual assessment depends on destination, dates, bite exposure, symptoms, testing and prior dengue history.
Chikungunya is transmitted to humans mainly by infected Aedes mosquitoes.
Common features include fever and joint pain, which can be prolonged.
Mosquito-bite avoidance is the main preventive measure for most travellers.
Risk varies by destination, outbreak activity, season and travel behaviour.
Travellers should use repellent, cover skin and reduce mosquito entry into sleeping areas.
People who become ill after travel should seek medical advice and provide their travel history.
UKHSA monitors imported cases and assesses the risk of local transmission.
Invasive-mosquito surveillance supports preparedness for vector-borne disease.
A destination advisory or mosquito detection does not prove that a traveller has chikungunya.
Diagnosis and risk assessment require symptom, travel, exposure and laboratory evidence.
